newsitem.title: UK: UK white Christmas could severely harm sugar beets.
newsitem.headline: UK white Christmas could severely harm sugar beets.

text.p: British Sugar warned farmers on Thursday that severe frosts forecast for the coming weekend could damage sugar beets in unprotected clamps, especially where freshly harvested, the company said in a statement. Regional weather forecasts predicted air temperatures as low as minus four degrees Celsius (25 degrees Fahrenheit) and ground temperatures would be correspondingly lower, it said.
"The cold weather is expected to move across the country from the north west, pushing the current warm weather ahead of it," it said.

"The duration of this cold weather will depend on the battle between the cold and warm fronts but it is expected that it will result in a "white' Christmas." It noted that the British beet crop had suffered severe damage in previous years from similar conditions, costing growers around three million pounds ($4.98 million).

A British Sugar official said 19 percent of the crop was still waiting to be lifted as of last weekend, compared with 15 percent at the same stage in the 1995/96 campaign. The crop's average sugar content stood at 18.10 percent, up from last year's 16.60 percent reported for equivalent stage. Up to 10 percent of beets would probably still be in the ground into next week, he added.
"The campaign is going well...but there is a risk of frost over the weekend," he said.

Last week, the National Farmers Union (NFU) voiced concern over the amount of beet which remained to be lifted due to the larger harvest, as in previous years all the crop would have been lifted by this stage.
Any beet left in the ground at this stage will run the risk of frost damage and will then be unable to enter British Sugar's factories for processing.
The company official said 51 percent of beets had already been delivered for processing, compared with 55 percent last year, with 29 percent still on farms or in clamps after 30 percent in 1995/96.

This year's campaign started late to give beets more chance to develop and take advantage of mild autumn weather. But the late start has meant more risk to the crop as a whole because a higher percentage of beets will still have to be lifted.

Britain is widely expected to turn in a larger sugar production from its 1996/97 crop, possibly as much as 1.50 million tonnes in raw value terms compared with 1.33 million from the previous campaign.
